title: The Mahabharata
subtitle: The Bharata epic

description: At 1.8 million words, the Mahabharata is the longest poem in the world. A war between cousins, a coachman god, and a lesson in duty.

hero.hook: Ten times Homer, a war of cousins, and a god who drives a chariot.

blocks.text: The **Mahabharata** is not a novel. It is the longest epic poem ever composed: approximately **1.8 million words**, or ten times the Iliad and the Odyssey combined. Its Sanskrit title means "the great story of the Bharatas", a royal lineage of ancient India.

In the center: a fratricidal war for the throne of, mythical capital of the North. Two branches of the same family are tearing each other apart. In the midst of the chaos, a sacred dialogue changes everything: the [[Hastinapura]], one of the most widely read texts in Hinduism. [[Bhagavad Gita (Concept)]]

sections.title: The genesis of an encyclopedia of the soul

blocks.text: The Mahabharata is attributed to the sage **Vyasa**, both author and character of the story. In reality, the text was formed over nearly eight centuries, between **400 BC.** and **400 AD**, from a long oral tradition.

blocks.caption: Vyasa, the legendary sage credited with the Mahabharata.

blocks.text: According to legend, Vyasa dictated so quickly that the god **Ganesha** broke one of his tusks to use it as a stylus and not lose anything.

The work has **18 parvas** (books) and approximately **100, 000** couplets. It's not just a war: it's a [[Somme]] of Indian knowledge, politics, morality, cosmology, embedded myths. There is a saying: “What is not in the Mahabharata is nowhere. » We also see the transition from ancient Vedic religion to classical . [[Brahmanism]]

On one side, the five brothers **Pandava**, sons of King Pandu, models of virtue. On the other, the hundred **Kaurava**, sons of the blind king **Dhritarashtra**, led by the ambitious **Duryodhana**. A rigged dice game ruins the Pandavas: they lose their kingdom and go into exile for thirteen years.

blocks.caption: The battle of Kurukshetra, the warlike heart of the Mahabharata.

blocks.text: On their return, **Krishna**, prince of the Yadavas and ally of the Pandavas, attempts mediation. The Kauravas refuse. War breaks out on the plain of **Kurukshetra** and lasts **18 days**. Masters against students, cousins ​​against cousins: it is , moral duty, which comes into conflict with blood. The Pandavas win, but the warrior caste is almost wiped out. [[Dharma]]

sections.title: The sacred dialogue of the Bhagavad-Gita

blocks.text: Just before the first shock, the archer **Arjuna**, the most formidable of the Pandavas, sees his uncles, his friends, his masters in the enemy ranks. He drops his bow. His coachman, **Krishna** (avatar of the god Vishnu), then responds to him in the **Bhagavad-Gita**: approximately **700** verses on duty and action.

blocks.caption: Krishna guides Arjuna on the chariot, to the threshold of battle.

blocks.text: In 1945, the physicist **Robert Oppenheimer**, who had learned Sanskrit, quoted Krishna after the first atomic test: “Now I have become Death, the destroyer of worlds. »

Krishna teaches **Karma Yoga**: to act according to one's duty, without clinging to the fruits of action. Kurukshetra then becomes the mirror of an inner struggle. The battlefield also speaks of consciousness.

The Mahabharata shaped the ethics of Southeast Asia. In the 20th century, **Gandhi** read the Bhagavad-Gita as a “dictionary of conduct”, making war an allegory of inner struggle. The theater of **Peter Brook** and huge Indian series brought the epic to hundreds of millions of spectators.
Why does the text last? Because he refuses simple answers. It confronts everyone with impossible choices, and makes the battlefield the mirror of conscience.
The **Mahabharata**, the world's longest poem, recounts the war of **Kurukshetra** between Pandava and Kaurava, and houses the **Bhagavad-Gita**, where Krishna teaches selfless action and **Dharma**.
